claims.claim: The Czech Republic has no wealth tax

sources.name: PwC: Czech Republic, other taxes
sources.says: Last reviewed 27 July 2026. "There are no net wealth/worth taxes in the Czech Republic." "There is no inheritance tax." "Gifts are not taxed by a special gift tax, but rather they are included in the recipient's PIT", with an exemption for gifts from close relatives (not defined on the page).

sources.name: PwC quick chart: net wealth/worth tax rates
sources.says: Georgia: "NA" (last reviewed 02 September 2026); Hungary: "N/A" (01 July 2026); Czech Republic: "NA" (27 July 2026); Turkey: "NA" (09 September 2026). The page defines NA as "the territory does not have the indicated tax or requirement".

claims.claim: Residents are taxed on worldwide income

sources.name: PwC: Czech Republic, taxes on personal income
sources.says: Last reviewed 27 July 2026. "Czech tax residents are generally subject to Czech income tax on their worldwide income." Gross annual income up to CZK 1,762,812 (36 times the average monthly salary) is taxed at 15% and income above it at 23%. "A special tax base with the rate of 15% applies to selected types of non-Czech investment income"; the taxpayer may opt for it, and allowances cannot reduce that base.

claims.claim: Foreign dividends and bond interest can go in a separate base at a flat 15% (otherwise 15%/23%)

sources.name: PwC: Czech Republic, taxes on personal income

sources.name: PwC: Czech Republic, income determination
sources.says: Last reviewed 27 July 2026. Foreign dividend and interest income "can be included in the separate tax base, which is subject to a flat 15% tax rate". Time test for exempt capital gains: "three years for direct ownership of securities". From 1 January 2026 "the annual limit of CZK 40 million for exemption of income from the sale of securities" is abolished where the time test is met; the limit still applies to transactions closed in 2025 and continues for cryptocurrencies.

claims.note: Also the tagline ("a 15% dividend option") and the summary. The 23% band starts at CZK 1,762,812 on the page reviewed July 2026.

claims.claim: The route is a long-term visa for "other purposes": up to 12 months, decided in 90–120 days, with a purpose statement, modest proof of funds, housing and €400k+ health insurance

sources.name: Czech Embassy in Tel Aviv: long-term visa for other purposes
sources.says: Published 17.06.2020, last updated 01.02.2024. "The visa for a stay over 90 days is granted for a maximum length of 12 months." "The processing of long term visas for other purposes takes up from 90 to 120 days." Purpose is shown by an invitation, a notarised statement or a detailed written explanation. Funds: "at least 15 x 3 130 CZK" for the first month plus twice 3,130 CZK for each further month (CZK 78,250 for six months). Accommodation must be proved. Health insurance: at least EUR 400,000 per insured event with no co-payment, from Pojišťovna VZP or another insurer active in the Czech Republic. Retirees are not mentioned.

sources.name: Czech Embassy in Washington: LT visa, other purposes
sources.says: Published 10 May 2016, last updated 20 September 2024. For "all other types of long stay (for over 90 days of stay) visas"; processing takes "from 90 to 120 days"; all visas must be approved by the Czech Ministry of Interior. Funds: 15 times the existential minimum of CZK 3,130 for the first month plus double it for each later month. Lists travel medical insurance without an amount. Retirees are not mentioned, and the page does not say whether there is a right to the visa.

claims.note: Two embassy pages (Tel Aviv, updated February 2024; Washington, updated September 2024). The Interior Ministry's portal ipc.gov.cz lists long-term visa purposes without a general "other" entry; the embassy pages and the Bogotá embassy page (updated June 2025, read, not listed) do. Funds for a year work out to about CZK 116,000. Whether a retiree's stated purpose is accepted is at the ministry's discretion and no page speaks of retirees.
